caption_en: 246. Room (58), S wall, section E: vignette with cupid with the attributes of Hera, the dove, the crown and a hydna. IV style.

247. Room (58), S wall, section E, upper area: squared carpet borders with acroterial birds and metal vase, crowning the side panel of the middle area. This is followed by the yellow frame with pods, above which is a leafy pergola, which supports a high floral spire from which flowering branches emerge. Inside the pergola, resting on a candelabrum, is a figure; on the sides are two eagles with spread wings resting on candelabra, from which arched garlands branch off; other garlands hang from the cusp and it supports a small picture with cupid € vase; again, on the sides of the cusp are two swans and two oblique thyrsis rest on the pergola.

248. Room (58), S wall, section E, upper area: the painted stucco frieze (here on a blue background with marine animals in white), the stucco frame with pods, the black frieze with carpet edges, crossed thyrsis and arched garlands. IV style.

249. Room (58), S wall, middle area, central section: painting with Narcissus seated and a cupid pouring water into a basin. The story of the young man and the fatal element of his deception are not represented in full, but are alluded to through the associations aroused by the presence of water. The position of Narci1072

251. Room (58), S wall, section E: vignette with the attributes of Apollo (cupid resting the lyra near a high tripod, on the ground is the zither). Due to the almost complete fall of color, the motif can only be read thanks to the engraved sketch. IV style.
250. Room (58), S wall, central section: upper black area with a floral spire rising from a crater, surmounted by a winged figure. IV style.
252. Room (58), wall W, open to the antechamber (57), with the walls covered with rough plaster.

253. Room (58): fragments relocated în situ of the ceiling, with a black background like the walls and the floor. The central element of the lowered vault, arranged around an octagon, is adapted to the size of the room by the rectangular bands along the side walls (cf. Barbet 1985, pp. 242-243). IV style.

254. Room (58): detail of the ceiling with a central octagon bordered by a garland, containing a chariot (in which were perhaps attributes of divinities?). The octagon is inscribed within a second octagon, which is in turn inscribed within a square; In the waste fields, eagles arranged in front of oblique lines that trace the diagonals of the square accentuate the effect of a coffered ceiling. IV style.

255. Corridor (59): threshold E, in black and white mosaic (cord within a white rectangular carpet) with marble slabs on three sides. The walls of the room can be glimpsed, simply plastered as in all the service rooms of the underground floor.

256. Corridor (59): black and white mosaic floor with threshold N in the foreground, which leads to the room (57), with hexagons outlined in white on a black background, and in the background the threshold of entrance to the hall (62), with rectangles containing diamonds and squares inscribed within diamonds. Visible, at the top, is the edge of the opus sectile floor of the hall (62), in squares of black limestone alternating with strips of palombino.
257. Corridor (59), section E: vault made up of clay pipes, covered with rough plaster (Kockel AA 1986, p. 511).

258. Apsidal hall (62), overlooking the terrace (56) with a view of the gulf through three large windows: the room retains only the imprints of the opus sectile floor (from the late Republican age?), which in the apse had bands of triangular tiles of different heights, and in the room square tiles whose side measured a foot; the overall effect naturally also had to count on the alternation of colors. Since in the room (as in all the floors below) there seems to be no trace of the passage of the Bourbon excavators (a circumstance confirmed by the discovery of various furnishings, including coverings of triclinary beds: Maiuri BdA 1961; Kockel AA 1986, p. 512, fig. 43 and note 264; B. Conticello, in Rediscovering Pompeii, p. 256, n. 180), it is probable that the removal of the pavement slabs took place already in ancient times (examples of ancient spoliation are cited several times in eighteenth-century reports: cf. for example Fiorelli, PAH I, p. '79, in which it is sometimes also significantly specified when these did not take place: ibid., p. 87).

259. Apsidal hall (62), N wall, section W, with the sequence of the doors of the rooms overlooking the sea on the first floor below: fresco of the fourth style with a black background; The fresco rests on the edge of the opus sectile floor and leans against the marble covering of the plinth.

260. Apsidal hall (62), detail of fig. Previous: Black upper area with porch with hanging garland and acroterium in the shape of a stylized dolphin. The fresco of the fourth style is executed on the masonry in opus reticulata.

The corner must have been covered with wood, resting on a marble plinth, still preserved, and apparently older than the fresco decoration of the fourth style.
262. Apsidal living room (62), N wall: the room continues the series of monochrome walls in the fourth style that characterizes the first floor below the house.

264. Apsidal hall (62), N wall, section W: at the foreshortening of the middle area there is a Satyr, who carries a goat on his left shoulder and has the pedum in his right. IV style.

266. Apsidal hall (62), N wall, central section: priestly helmet hanging from a garland stretched at the base of the panel contained within the central aedicule. IV style.

274. Apsidal hall (62), wall E, section N: at the base of the side panel of the middle area is a bucranium from which garlands branch off. IV style.

276. Apsidal hall (62), wall E, section N: the lower part of the architectural foreshortening, with staircase and open door. IV style.
278. Apsidal hall (62), wall E, section N: in the upper area there is a female figure resting on a candelabrum, holding garlands in her hands. IV style.

279. Apsidal hall (62), E wall, central section. Despite the different interpretation of Elijah (Elia RM 1962), or the doubts that have recently been raised (Hij mans 1995), the traditional interpretation of the scene as Sternenstreit, i.e. as a contention between the star of day and night before Apollo, seems to be the one that best suits both the attributes of the characters represented and the context of the scene (cf. E. Simon,  in LIMC, II, p. 421, n. 421, s.v. Apollon/Apollo), which does not necessarily have to reflect the literarily attested version of a myth. Another recent reading proposal (Leach 1991) modifies the traditional identification and seeks the meaning of the scene also through the relationship with the other paintings in the environment and with the possible associations that their combination and the iconographic signs present in them could arouse in the observer: the identification of the characters with Phaethon and Aphrodite would allude to the union between the two,  the cause of Phaeton's fatal race on the chariot of Helios and therefore an inauspicious, 'inappropriate' union between a goddess and a mortal, placed in opposition to the scenes on the side walls, representing 'positive' unions between gods and mortals. This painting is also recessed with respect to the surrounding fresco.

The fresco of the fourth style leans both against the edge of the opus sectile floor and against the marble covering of the plinth, present in the corner.

295. Apsidal hall (62), S wall, section O: wall decoration of the fourth style with a black background. A preserved section of the edge of the opus sectile floor is visible, with square black limestone tiles with palombino strips.

297. Apsidal hall (62), W wall with the apse opened by three large windows with marble windowsill. Plinth: central panel with candelabra and stretched garlands, and side panels with hanging garlands and carpet edges, separated by narrow compartments with rampant animals. In the middle area, between the windows, are narrow panels.

298. Corridor (63), threshold E, in black and white mosaic: white mat with cord containing a square in the centre and ending with two transversal elements. Visible is the floor of black tesserae arranged in an oblique warp, with a border of black and white bands and a marginal flounce of black tesserae, and the marble slabs, with holes for the hinges (inserted later?). The floors of this part of the house seem to have been laid out all in a single phase, still attributable to the late Republican age.

299. The carpet floor of black tesserae arranged in an oblique warp of the corridor (63), with the threshold of the apsidal hall (62) in the background and, in the foreground, the threshold of the room (64). The walls of the corridor are covered with rough plaster.

300. Detail of fig. with the threshold between the corridor (63) and the room (64), flanked by marble slabs (inserted later ?) with holes for the hinges. The slender floral motif contained within a square (a four-petaled flower inserted within a circle, with four axial palmettes) finds comparison in the repertoire of the III style and is probably located between the Republican age and the imperial age.

301. Room (64): detail of the carpet floor of black tesserae arranged in an oblique warp bordered by black and white bands; the marginal flounce is of black tesserae in an oblique warp. The monochrome application of the floor contrasts with the wall decoration (more recent), which in the middle and upper areas has large monochrome fields, but with a red background.

302. Room (64), N wall: plinth and plinth, the latter with large panels with garlands separated by avant-corps with plants. The red middle area has a large aedicule with a painting in the center, which wide architectural views separate from the side panels with medallions. The upper area, also red, is very poorly preserved. The polychrome stucco frame is made of lotuses and palmettes. IV style.

303. Room (64), N wall, central section: the painting with the nymph at the bath, spied on by an old Silenus looking out above the cave, derives from the contemporary figurations of Diana at the bath observed by Actaeon (Leach RM 1981, fig. 134, 2). The change of the protagonists accentuates the erotic connotation of the scene, already present in some contemporary redactions of the mythological episode.

304. Room (64), wall E: in the black plinth, the centre of the wall is underlined by a large panel with deer and garlands between two foreparts with plants; in the side panels are carpet borders and taut garlands. The middle area also emphasizes the center of the wall, occupied by an aedicule between wide views and further highlighted by the presence of a larger mythological painting of the still life paintings of the side panels. IV style.
305. Room (64), wall E, central section: plinth and black plinth, with hanging garlands and rampant deer flanked by foreparts with plants. IV style.
306. Room (64), wall E, central section: painting with Narcissus in the centre of the middle area. The subject is the most frequent on walls decorated in the IV style.
307. Room (64), wall E, section S: in the side panel of the middle area, on a red background, there is a rather poor picture, with a still life with figs and dates.

308. Room (64), S wall, section E: black plinth, black plinth with a large panel with situle hanging from garlands and large foreparts with plants; red middle area with a panel bordered by carpet edges between large architectural views. IV style.
309. Room (64), S wall, section E: medallion with architectural landscape in the middle area.

310. Room (64), wall W: the large window with a marble sill, open to the landscape in front, was framed by a wooden frame, around which the wall decoration stops. On the black background of the floor and plinth, the red background of the middle area, the upper area and the bezel stands out. IV style.
311. Room (64), O wall, N section: small picture with still life in the red panel of the middle area.

312. Cubicle (67), black and white mosaic floor: the arrangement of the thresholds marking the floor shows that here there must have been a cubicle with two alcoves, which had an access in the S section (see fig. below). The antechamber has a carpet of white tesserae arranged in an oblique warp with a border of black and white bands and a marginal flounce of white tesserae arranged in an oblique warp; the alcove E has bedside rugs with swastika meanders alternating with squares containing triangles with opposite steps for the vertices. The same motif (stepped triangles) adorns the bedside rug of alcove S (68), which can be glimpsed in the background (see fig. 314). Technique and ornamentation are typical of the floors assigned to the II style, in which the sober two-tone ornamentation contrasts with the chromatic variety of the wall decoration schemes, particularly rich in these rooms for private use. 78 N45219

313. Cubicle (67), threshold S: mat of white tesserae arranged in an oblique warp with dotted crosses of black tesserae. The threshold, which can be assigned to the II style, is cut by the O wall, of which on the right, at the top, a remnant of the cladding can be glimpsed.
314. Cubicle (67), alcove S (68), floor: carpet of white tesserae arranged in an oblique warp; bedside rugs with rows of overlapping stepped triangles within a checkerboard edge. II style.

315. Cubicle (67), alcove S (68): in the S-E corner there is a remnant of the decoration of the second style. Above the black plinth, the plinth has the imitation of a covering of raised marble slabs, with orthostats arranged at the head that take up a veined yellow marble alternating with orthostats arranged in purple cut. The fragment ends with a yellow molded frame, above which the middle area must have begun.

316. Cubicle (67), alcove S (68): fragments relocated in situ of the decoration of The style of the wall O, which differs in the details of the plinth from that reproduced in fig. previous. In the middle area, above the moulded cornice, fragments of ashlars. The subtle light and dark brushstrokes simulate the light and shadow parts of raised slabs and increase the effect of architectural illusion that is the basis of the decorative schemes of the late Republican age.

317. Room (71), view from O. We do not know the reasons why the second style decoration of wall E and the adjoining sections of the side walls, still in an excellent state of preservation — at least judging by what has been preserved — was later obliterated by a cavity built in front of it, which restricted the room. Another decorative scheme of the second style was made on this cavity and, at an even later stage (see fig. below), access to the room was blocked by closing the wall O.

319. Room (71), N-E corner: fresco of the second style belonging to the oldest phase preserved here. To the left of the corner pillar, which emphasizes the structure of the room, there is a partition. On the right is the complex multi-storey architectural framework overlooked by the figure of Venus: a partition surmounted by clypei frames a tetrastyle temple with Corinthian capitals. On the façade, above a closed door, the overdoor is adorned with stars and crescent moons (cf. Kockel AA 1986, note 263).

320. Room (71), wall E, central section: from the open door of the temple, adorned with metal studs and flanked by overdoors with stars and crescent moons (cf. the bibl. cit. in the previous fig.), a crowned and veiled Venus looks out, with cupid on her shoulder. If, as has been suggested by many (cf. most recently Zevi 1996), the houses with II style decorations in Pompeii and the villas in the suburbs with these decorative schemes are to be referred to the most important figures of the Silla colony, this painting, centered on the figure of Venus, "the 'personal' divinity of the dictator" (Zevi, cit.), must have had a value and a meaning that went far beyond the feeling of magical estrangement that it communicates to our eyes.

322. Room (71), SE corner: in the upper area of the decoration belonging to the oldest phase there is a small picture with doors in which, despite the extreme speed of execution, warriors, children and female figures can be recognized near a tent and ships in the background.

Room (71), S wall: as on the cavity that covered the wall with the figure of Venus, also in the center of the S wall, framed by a column avant-corps and preceded by a staircase, is a half-open door framing a censer, above which hangs a lamp holder, only partially preserved (on the chandelier that adorns one of the walls of the Villa di Boscoreale preserved in the Museum of Naples rests an erote).

325. Room (72): the section of floor that acts as an antechamber to the room with the figure of Venus (71). Mosaic carpet of white tesserae arranged in an oblique warp with dotted black tesserae; low threshold adorned with a row of stepped diamonds, within which are crosses of black tesserae; checkerboard edge. In the photo you can also see the infill of the W side of the room (71), which covered the original jambs covered with white stucco. The floor belongs to the same phase of the second style attested in the surrounding rooms (67), (68) and (71).

They use tuff drums of different origins for the lower part and tuff and bricks for the rest of the elevation; they were covered with red stucco on the lower part and white on the upper part. Duban, (PParigi, Cat. no. 64) executed between 1823 and 1828, the period of his stay in Rome as president of the French Academy, reveals that the walls were painted with yellow panels squared in red (fig. 3b).

Duban (PParigi, Cat. no. 63). The carpet consists of a network of octagons and white squares on a black background, with a white square in the center of each octagon. The marginal flounce is white with tesserae arranged in a straight warp.

17. Triclinium (n): the room, which flanked the tablinum (k) and was open to the S, preserved on the wall O the decoration of the IV style documented by Mazois (Mazois, II, Tav. XXIII, 14), and by a watercolour by Duban (PParigi, Cat. 67, which gives it incomplete at the right end). Due to the collapse of the floor, the underlying room (Q) can be seen in the photograph. The red plinth exhibited flowering bushes in the side panels, in the central one two edges of carpet arranged like semi-aedicules with acroterial volutes on the sides of a corolla, and in the compartments corollas between palmettes; the middle area had a paratactic structure with blue panels separated by compartments with a red background crossed by grotesque candelabra. Grotesque bands were also found horizontally delimiting the side panels that contained medallions, with a cupid and a deer on the left, a cupid catching a dove with a ribbon on the right, clear allusions, considering that a third, again documented by Mazois, depicted a cupid with a peacock, to Diana, Venus and Juno. The central painting depicts the group of a Satyr and a Maenad derived from the same model as in a painting in the House of Wounded Adonis (VI 7, 18: cf. vol. IV, p. 406) with the young man grasping the woman from the back, holding her by the arms, while turning her gaze towards him; in the background on the left was the statue of Priapus.

The upper part of the candelabrum recalls in its oval shape the lotus buds of the band separating the middle area.

64. Triclinium (6), vault. Niccolini's panel reconstructs the scheme of the decoration of the vault with a combination of lozenges, triangles and squares outlined in red and yellow on a black background to obtain a design of stars within dodecagons. Palmettes and small four-petaled corollas, in the center of the geometric elements, complete the decoration.  from Niccolini, IV, Tav. VII (Fot. Rossi-ni) 224

Triclinium (6): detail of the N-W section of the vault with one of the perforated medallions that interrupt the decorative motif and that were perhaps used to drop petals, perfumes or other things from above on the diners, according to an extremely luxurious fashion, as described by Suetonius (Suet., Nero, VI, 31) with regard to the Domus Aurea.
